We found that the models achieved a superior classification accuracy, exceeding 98%, when trained on raw or minimally processed images. Conversely, the application of aggressive, multi-stage filtering combinations resulted in a significant degradation of performance, reducing accuracy by as much as 15%. This decline is attributed to the inadvertent removal of subtle but vital pathological features, which these sophisticated networks are otherwise capable of learning directly. This study conclusively demonstrates that for robust CNNs and high-quality image data, elaborate preprocessing is not only unnecessary but detrimental.

title: Potato Leaf Disease Detection System
abstract: Early Blight (Alternaria solani) and Late Blight are two diseases that significantly impair the production of potatoes, one of the most significant food crops in the world. (Infestans phytopf). If these infections are not identified and treated in a timely manner, they may result in significant yield losses. Manual inspection and laboratory testing are the mainstays of traditional disease detection techniques, which are frequently labor-intensive and slow. Faster and more precise detection systems may now be created because to recent developments in web technologies, machine learning, and image processing.This study examines the various methodologies, including both conventional and contemporary AI-based technologies, for identifying Early Blight and Late Blight in potatoes. It also explains A web-based detection system that use a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to diagnose diseases from leaf photos was created with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Express.js. In order to assist farmers in better crop management, the study outlines the advantages, difficulties, and potential future developments for enhancing potato disease detection.

title: Detection of Rice Leaf Diseases Using Transfer Learning Architectures: A Comparative Analysis
abstract: Rice (Oryza sativa L.) productivity is frequently reduced by leaf diseases such as Bacterial Leaf Blight, Brown Spot, Blast, and Tungro, causing major yield losses and threatening food security. To improve early disease recognition, this study develops and evaluates five hybrid deep learning architectures that integrate pre-trained Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), including GRU, LSTM, and BiLSTM units. A publicly available dataset containing 3,700 images across five disease categories was preprocessed through normalization and data augmentation to enhance generalization. Among the evaluated models, the DenseNet201+GRU hybrid achieved the best performance with $\mathbf{9 9. 0 \%}$ test accuracy, $\mathbf{9 8. 7 \%}$ precision, $\mathbf{9 8. 8 \%}$ recall, and an overall $\mathbf{F 1}$-score of $\mathbf{9 8. 8 \%}$, outperforming the standalone CNN baselines. These results demonstrate that incorporating RNN layers to capture sequential spatial dependencies within feature maps can significantly improve automated rice leaf disease classification. The proposed method provides a robust and scalable solution for real-time smart agriculture applications.

title: Real-Time Coconut Tree Disease Detection and Management Using YOLOv8
Attention-Augmented RT-DETR-L for Real-Time Multi-Class Grape Leaf Disease Classification
Hybrid Optimized AgriShieldNet Framework for an Interpretable Multi‐Crop Leaf Disease Classification
abstract: ABSTRACT Early detection of plant leaf diseases is essential for improving crop productivity, reducing financial losses, and enhancing sustainability in modern agricultural practices. However, most automated systems struggle to accurately capture diverse morphological variations of plant leaf diseases across multiple crop types, while manual inspection methods are time‐consuming, labor‐intensive, and prone to human error. To address these challenges, this paper proposes Hy‐OptiASNet, a hybrid optimized deep learning framework for interpretable multi‐crop leaf disease classification. The proposed framework utilizes EfficientNet‐B0 for robust spatial feature extraction; a Long Short‐Term Memory (LSTM) network is employed to model sequential feature dependencies and improve structured feature learning, followed by a Morphology‐Aware Vision Embedding (MAVE) module to enhance representation of fine‐grained morphological disease patterns. In addition, a novel Sandpiper Optimization Algorithm (SPOA) is incorporated for feature refinement and hyperparameter optimization, thereby improving generalization capability and classification stability. To enhance interpretability, visualization techniques are used to highlight biologically relevant disease regions, enabling improved understanding of model decisions. Extensive experiments were conducted on multi‐crop datasets consisting of apple, tomato, and grape leaf images. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed Hy‐OptiASNet framework achieves classification accuracies of 98.98%, 98.21%, and 98.35% for apple, tomato, and grape datasets, respectively, outperforming several existing state‐of‐the‐art methods. These findings indicate that the proposed framework provides an effective and reliable solution for precision agriculture and real‐world plant disease monitoring applications.

title: Smart Agriculture System for Tea Plant Disease Detection and Targeted Pesticide Recommendation
abstract: Tea leaf cultivation has significant importance in the agricultural economies of many developing countries. However, tea leaf productivity is influenced by diseases like blister blight, red rust, bird’s eye spot, etc., and environmental factors like leaf scorch. Conventional disease detection techniques often include manual inspection, which is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. Moreover, this technique may also lead to inaccurate results. In this research work, a novel approach has been proposed to develop a tea leaf disease detection and pesticide recommendation system using advanced deep learning concepts. In this work, the YOLO12 framework has been implemented to detect tea leaf diseases. This framework utilizes the advantage of both lightweight and strong YOLO models to detect tea leaf diseases in real-time with high accuracy. In this research work, a knowledge-based recommendation system has also been integrated to provide recommendations to the users based on the diseases detected. In this work, the proposed model has been trained using a diverse dataset of tea leaf images. An accuracy of 96.7% has been achieved by the proposed model, proving its capability to generalize accurately. In this work, a user-friendly web interface has been implemented to make the system accessible to users.

title: Adaptive Online LoRA Control Loop for Plant Disease Recognition with Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Multimodal vision–language models (VLMs) are promising for plant disease recognition, but practical deployment across many crops still suffers from crop-specific, trial-and-error low-rank adaptation (LoRA) tuning. We propose an adaptive online LoRA control loop that views LoRA parameters as a capacity budget, reallocates per-layer ranks and scaling factors using a first-order sensitivity measure, and performs lightweight online updates on crop-specific support sets. Experiments on multiple crops from the PlantVillage dataset show consistent improvements over manually tuned LoRA and over a Manual+CLIP baseline, indicating that importance-aware online adaptation complements the automatic selection of support sets. The study is restricted to clean, controlled images; extending the framework and ablations to field conditions and more diverse datasets is left for future work.

title: Crop Sentinel: AI-based Flood and Pest Damage Detection using Remote Sensing
abstract: Food security and farmer’s livelihoods are greatly affected globally by crop losses caused by flooding and pest infestations. CropSentinel is an AI (artificial intelligence) based framework developed for detecting damage to crops from flooding or pest infestations and will use remote sensing imagery as well as deep learning models to classify damaged crops based on these two conditions (flooding and/or pest infestation) compared to healthy crop conditions. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) with Transfer Learning will be utilized as a method of efficiently extracting features and improving overall classification performance. The data will be preprocessed using different methods such as image augmentation techniques; and the model will be evaluated using various performance metrics (i.e.: accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score). The result of this study will provide farmers, agricultural officials, and disaster management personnel with real time assessments of crop damage that will allow them to make informed decisions regarding recovery efforts related to flooding and pest-infested crops. CropSentinel illustrates the use of artificial intelligence as applied to precision agriculture, developing sustainable systems for monitoring crops, and creating resilient farming systems.

title: Design and Performance Evaluation of a CNN–Vision Transformer Hybrid Model for Plant Disease Classification
abstract: Leaf diseases in plants can significantly impact crop yields and may even cause severe financial loss. Hence, early and accurate detection of such diseases in plants plays an important role in agricultural practices. Although deep learning has shown significant improvement in detecting plant diseases, identifying visual details as well as leaf patterns simultaneously in an accurate manner remains a challenge. In consideration of such a problem, this research aims to develop a model based on a hybrid deep learning approach that combines Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and a Vision Transformer (ViT) for plant disease classification. The model has shown promising results in the Apple and Corn leaf datasets available publicly. The experimental results have achieved a high training accuracy rate of 99.8%, and a high validation accuracy rate of 98.7%. Also, the model has exhibited good learning behavior and accurate classification results.

title: RP-OCNN: A Hybrid Squeeze-Excitation Residual Network for Fine-Grained Rose Petal Condition Classification
abstract: Automated grading of fresh produce and floriculture has grown to be a very essential parameter due to the need of uniform post harvest quality and less labor force. Conventional quality control practices tend to be subjective and not able to detect minute early-stage indications of degradation or disease. The paper presents Rose Petal Optimized Convolutional neural Network (RP-OCNN) a new deep neural network architecture that is being specifically designed to perform the fine-grained classification of Dutch rose petals that has three important classes of conditions: Fresh, Dry, and Diseased. The RP-OCNN is designed based on a developed ResNet architecture with customized, slim, Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) attention blocks between each residual unit. This architectural change enables the adaptive channel-wise feature recalibration where the network decides to focus on the texture and color patterns that are critical in separating between these subtle visual conditions. The RP-OCNN trained on the imbalanced RoseVisulas dataset of 1,995 high-resolution images was found to reach a test set overall accuracy of 95.67 percent and a weighted F1-score of 95.78%. Weighted loss and SE-attention showed great success in improving performance on the minority 'Diseased' class, with a superior generalization performance to the current general-purpose models. The RP-OCNN is an effective, powerful and available device of real time quality management in commercial horticulture.

title: The causal effect of iterative changes in table tennis rules on the technical and tactical system: An empirical test based on Markov chain and decision tree models
abstract: This study examines the dynamic impact of recent reforms in table tennis, particularly innovations in ball material, competition time, and service rules, on the sport's technical and tactical evolution. Previous research has largely focused on isolated rule changes, lacking a systemic framework for causal inference. This study integrates a difference-in-differences model, Markov chain, and decision tree algorithm to explore the interplay between rule adjustments, technical compensation, and equilibrium reconstruction. Empirical analysis using multi-period data from top-level international competitions reveals that: increased ball diameter reduces scoring efficiency, shifting focus to multi-shot stability; the eleven-point system accelerates tactical radicalization but increases risk during critical points; and rule changes in unobstructed service enhance the diffusion of receiving techniques. The findings highlight nonlinear threshold effects and differentiated adaptation pathways shaped by equipment parameters, competition structure, and athlete technical styles. The study proposes strategies to improve stability during stalemate segments, enhance psychological training for high-pressure moments, and optimize equipment, offering insights for training, tactical design, and policy development in competitive table tennis.

title: Classification of Wheat Rust Disease Using MobileNetV2 Technology
venue: Springer proceedings in earth and environmental sciences

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) in Powering Digital Twins for Digital Plant Pathology
Image-based automated identification of SBR-transmitting planthoppers on sticky traps
venue: Journal of Plant Diseases and Protection
abstract: Abstract Accurate monitoring of insect vectors is critical for managing Syndrome ‘basses richesses’ (SBR), a disease affecting sugar beet crops in Europe. This study presents a deep learning (DL) approach for the automated identification of Cixiidae planthoppers, the primary SBR vectors. Several DL architectures, including convolutional neural networks (CNN) and vision transformers, were benchmarked, leading to the selection of Inception-v3. This architecture was then used to develop two complementary models: the first to distinguish Cixiidae from other insect groups, and the second to classify species within Cixiidae, namely Pentastiridius leporinus , Hyalesthes obsoletus , and Reptalus spp. Discrimination among these species is essential, as they differ in their efficiency and role in transmitting SBR. The models were trained and validated on over 40,000 high-resolution insect images collected from sticky traps deployed in sugar beet and grapevine fields across Germany and Serbia between 2022 and 2024. Species labels were based on morphological identification and verified via DNA barcoding, and the resulting dataset was made publicly available. Statistical and visual model evaluation confirmed high performance and biological relevance. The first model achieved 94% overall accuracy with a 99% recall for Cixiidae, while the second model exceeded 99% overall accuracy. Performance was further evaluated on unseen test traps from 2024, showing high agreement between manual and model counts (R 2 > 0.9). Analysis of image resolution identified 1,600 dpi as the optimal balance between performance and computational efficiency. This study demonstrates the potential of DL for reliable SBR-vector monitoring and scalable integration into precision pest management strategies.

title: AI-driven crop disease detection with efficient NetB3 hybrids for sustainable agriculture
abstract: In precision agriculture, crop disease detection can be a highly valuable undertaking in which scalable and correct solutions may save considerable amounts of money and loss of yield. This paper introduces a comparative analysis of state-of-the-art deep learning models with special attention to EfficientNetB3 hybrids, which are trained on a balanced subsample of the PlantVillage dataset with 33 classes based on nine crops. To overcome the shortcomings of the previous studies, which used unbalanced sample, a leakage-free balancing approach was used, resulting in 13,200 training and 3,300 validation samples. Custom head transfer learning was used where it was tested using two strategies; FreezeUnfreeze fine-tuning, and Singlephase training. MobileNetV2, InceptionV3, DenseNet121, GhostNet, in addition to other baseline CNNs, were compared to baseline Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The findings indicate that EfficientNetB3 hybrids are superior with an accuracy of ≥99.5% and 99.9% Area Under the Curve (AUC) and specificity than the previous CNN-based systems. The paper logically defines a performance ladder between model options and real-life deployment demands, such as lightweight mobile applications to precision agriculture systems, and points out future trends in the field-based validation.

title: PromptSAMNet: A memory-enhanced adaptive prompting and clustering-augmented SAM 2.0 framework for multi-leaf plant disease diagnosis
Benchmark Datasets for Satellite Image Time Series Classification: A Review
abstract: Recent advances in satellite missions, particularly the Landsat, Sentinel, and Gaofen series, have led to the rapid accumulation of high-quality remote sensing data with frequent revisits. As these data have become more widely available, Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) have become an important tool for monitoring Earth surface dynamics. SITS now supports a wide range of applications, including precision agriculture, Land Use/Cover Change (LULCC) monitoring, environmental management, and disaster response. This growth has also promoted the development of advanced SITS classification datasets. However, existing reviews have mainly focused on SITS classification algorithms or specific applications, while systematic comparisons of public SITS benchmark datasets remain limited. This lack of synthesis makes it difficult for researchers to navigate fragmented resources and select datasets that match specific scientific or operational tasks. To address this gap, this paper provides a comprehensive review and analysis of 29 publicly available medium-to-high-resolution SITS classification benchmark datasets released between 2017 and 2025. These datasets are intended for training, testing, and validating land-cover classification algorithms, rather than for direct use as operational map products. We conduct a detailed statistical and comparative analysis of these datasets, focusing on their key characteristics across spectral, temporal, and spatial dimensions, as well as their labeling systems. In addition, this review summarizes the SITS classification algorithms that have been developed and benchmarked using these datasets. Finally, we identify the main challenges in constructing and applying SITS classification datasets and discuss future research directions, particularly in data reconstruction, multimodal fusion, change analysis, and advanced model architectures. This survey provides the research community with a systematic overview of SITS classification benchmark datasets and aims to support continued progress in this rapidly developing field.

title: Banana Leaf Disease Prediction Using Machine Learning and Deep Learning Techniques
venue: Interdisciplinary Journal of AI Machine Learning & Data Science
abstract: Banana cultivation plays a critical role in global agriculture; however, its productivity is severely affected by various foliar diseases such as Sigatoka, Panama wilt and Banana Bunchy Top Disease (BBTD). Early detection of these diseases is essential to minimize yield loss and ensure sustainable agricultural practices. Traditional diagnostic approaches rely on manual inspection, which is often subjective, time-consuming and inaccessible to farmers in remote regions. This study presents a robust and automated framework for banana leaf disease prediction using both Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) techniques. The proposed system employs image-based analysis, incorporating preprocessing methods such as normalization, resizing and data augmentation. Classical ML models including Support Vector Machine (SVM), k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)and Random Forest are compared with deep learning architectures such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and transfer learning-based ResNet50. Experimental results demonstrate that deep learning models significantly outperform traditional ML approaches, achieving a maximum accuracy of 97.3% using ResNet50. The findings highlight the potential of AI-driven systems in enabling early disease detection and supporting precision agriculture.

title: A sustainable approach to plant disease detection using deep learning framework for energy-efficient agricultural consumer electronics
abstract: The increasing demand for agricultural productivity is challenged by plant diseases that have led to crop losses and significant financial impacts. Early detection of plant diseases can save critical resources and prevent further crop damage, ensuring sustainable agricultural practices. However, existing methods for plant disease classification often face limitations, including high computational costs, resource constraints, and internet dependency, especially in rural agricultural regions. To address these challenges, we propose a novel edge–cloud collaboration framework that integrates the optimized CNN model for accurate and energy-efficient plant disease classification. The framework leverages edge devices for local real-time processing to reduce latency and energy consumption while utilizing the cloud for computationally intensive tasks to ensure scalability and robustness. The proposed framework provides a collaborative processing mechanism in which the edge-enabled servers execute the feature extraction and preliminary classification tasks based on raw input while allowing the cloud server to aggregate and refine the global model. The customized CNN is of a lightweight design that can flexibly integrate both feature extraction and classification layers to achieve high accuracy with relatively low resource consumption. Key contributions in this work are a scalable architecture uniquely adapted to resource-constrained settings, an efficient CNN architecture for plant disease classification, and extensive evaluations across diverse datasets. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves up to 99.3% accuracy with 0.998 F1-score for the PlantVillage dataset, 97.12% accuracy with 0.971 F1-score on the Corn or Maize dataset, and 99.45% accuracy with 0.994 F1-score on the Potato leaf disease dataset. These results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed framework and its contribution to sustainable agricultural practices by enabling real-time, resource-efficient plant disease detection across various environments.

title: Detection of the mexR Gene in Pseudomonas aeruginosa During2 Arabidopsis Infection3456
abstract: Background: Pseudomonas aeruginosa species cause damage in various plant tissues by overcoming host defenses through the production of effectors and toxins. Pseudomonas aeruginosa infects Arabidopsis thaliana using multiple bacterial genes involved in virulence and adaptation. Objectives: The aim of this study was to identify the mexR gene in P. aeruginosa and investigate its potential role in infection and tissue damage in Arabidopsis thaliana Methods: Twelve plants per bacterial strain were used for infection assays. Disease symptoms were recorded daily to evaluate infection over a five-day period. The mexR gene was amplified from P. aeruginosa genomic DNA using PCR. Results: Water-soaking and yellow discoloration of infected leaves were observed two days after infection. An increase in colony-forming units (CFUs) was detected from day 0 to day 2, followed by only slight increases from day 2 to day 5. Out of fifteen P. aeruginosa strains tested, three strains were positive for the mexR gene. Conclusions: Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates exhibited a notable prevalence of the efflux pump regulatory gene mexR. This study provides evidence supporting an association between P. aeruginosa infection and tissue damage in Arabidopsis thaliana.

title: Easy to use and low cost leaf disease quantification workflow using Ilastik
abstract: Abstract Accurate and reproducible assessment of foliar disease severity is essential for evaluating the performance of heterogeneous plant communities and understanding host-pathogen interactions. However, traditional visual scoring methods remain subjective, with limited precision, and difficult to scale in large phenotyping experiments. Here, we present a semi-automated image analysis workflow designed to quantify multiple foliar disease symptoms simultaneously on wheat flag leaves sampled from varietal mixtures. The workflow combines three methodological components: (i) a standardized protocol for leaf sampling and imaging, (ii) supervised machine learning segmentation using Random Forest implemented in Ilastik to classify multiple symptoms (powdery mildew and yellow rust), and (iii) a graphical user interface facilitating pipeline deployment by non-specialist operators. To evaluate the influence of image representation on classification performance, four color spaces (RGB, HSV, HLS, LAB) were systematically compared. The approach was validated using images of durum wheat flag leaves collected from a field experiment assessing eight-way varietal mixtures under natural fungal pressure. Cross-validation against manually annotated images demonstrated high segmentation accuracy across all symptom. Comparison among color spaces revealed only minor differences in performance. Overall, this workflow offers a cost-effective, annotation-efficient and reproducible alternative to deep learning approaches, leveraging open-source and actively maintained tools while requiring limited training data and enabling objective, reproducible and scalable disease phenotyping.

title: Deep Learning-Based Plant Disease Detection: A CNN Approach for Accurate Diagnosis
venue: Lecture notes in networks and systems

title: Synthetic Data Augmented Leaflet-Level Ash Dieback Detection
Illumination-Decoupled Transformer Learning for Shadow-Robust Crop Disease Diagnosis Under Structured Cast Shadows
abstract: Crop disease diagnosis can be degraded by structured cast shadows, including panel-like strip shadows that motivate applications in agrivoltaic-style farming. This paper presents ShadowFormer-AV, a transformer-based framework that adapts general shadow-robust visual learning to crop disease classification by separating disease evidence from illumination interference. The proposed approach combines a soft shadow-prior extractor, an illumination-decoupled dual-stream token encoder, lesion-preserving adaptive attention, and a cross-view consistency objective between original and shadow-perturbed images. The method uses only standard RGB inputs and does not require shadow-free reference images, multispectral sensing, or pixel-level shadow annotation. We evaluated the framework on publicly available plant disease datasets using calibrated panel-like synthetic shadows and a naturally shadowed PlantDoc subset. Because no on-site agrivoltaic disease dataset was used, the conclusions were limited to shadow robustness under these simulated and naturally shadowed test conditions rather than verified performance under real photovoltaic-panel shadows. Within this validation boundary, ShadowFormer-AV improved accuracy, Macro-F1, and calibration over representative convolutional and transformer baselines, suggesting that illumination-aware token learning is useful for crop disease recognition under structured shadow interference.

title: Increasing plant density underpins greater root length density and root biomass of modern maize production
Integrating Envirotyping and Phenomics for AI-Enabled Multi-Environment Genomic Prediction in Crop Breeding
abstract: Genomic prediction is now routine in crop improvement, but its main bottleneck has shifted from marker density to environmental complexity. Breeders rarely need predictions for one fixed environment; they need to rank genotypes across target populations of environments that differ in weather, soils, management, and stress timing. This makes genotype-by-environment interaction a primary breeding problem rather than a secondary statistical nuisance. This review examines how genomic, environmental, and phenomic information can be integrated to improve multi-environment prediction in crop breeding pipelines. The review is narrative rather than PRISMA-style, but the literature search and selection logic were structured and explicitly defined. Peer-reviewed English-language studies were identified through structured searches of Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus, supplemented by backward citation screening, with emphasis on literature published from January 2023 to March 2026. Four conclusions emerge. First, environmental information is most useful when it is developmentally aligned, biologically interpretable, and matched to the target population of environments. Second, strong structured statistical baselines remain highly competitive, especially in moderate-sized or highly unbalanced datasets, whereas gains from more flexible machine-learning and deep-learning approaches are most evident in large, sparse, heterogeneous, and multimodal settings. Third, phenomic markers often improve prediction for complex traits, especially yield, because they capture realized crop responses not fully represented by markers alone. Fourth, practical value depends less on isolated gains in predictive accuracy than on evaluation under realistic deployment scenarios, including untested genotype and untested environment settings. Progress therefore requires transparent reporting, benchmark design, stage-aware envirotyping, multimodal integration, uncertainty reporting, and cost-aware deployment.

title: Using planetscope imagery to evaluate herbicide efficacy in maize (Zea mays) through post-application weed detection
abstract: Abstract Background Optimizing herbicide efficacy is increasingly critical due to the absence of new herbicide modes of action (MOA) and their widespread overuse. This study developed a satellite-based approach to map herbicide control failures for evaluating efficacy, based on the hypothesis that effective control reduces crop-weeds co-existence and thus spectral-spatial heterogeneity over time, whereas low efficacy increases it. Methods In controlled experimental maize plots (2022–2023), analysis of Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) multispectral imagery characterized weed-suppression dynamics following application of two herbicides with different MOA. Satellite imagery was processed to select gray-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) texture features sensitive to herbicide-induced pixel differences. Features selected were used to compare two satellite-based approaches for mapping herbicide control failures cover (%) across seven commercial maize fields: (i) a rule-based framework and (ii) UAV to satellite upscaling using a Random Forest model. Results Results showed that by 10 days after spraying (DAS), herbicide effects were uniformly expressed in both MOA, enabling separation between damaged and healthy weeds in UAV images. At the satellite scale, Near-Infrared (NIR)-based GLCM variance and mean were the most sensitive indicators of weed suppression. Using these features and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) from 10 and 14 DAS, a rule-based framework showed better performance compared to UAV to satellite upscaling, achieving within field precision and recall of 0.71 both, and between fields agreement with a coefficient of determination (R 2 ) of 0.97 and root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.86 (%). Conclusions These results demonstrate that rule-based GLCM framework provide an effective tool for evaluating herbicide control efficacy using PlanetScope satellite image.

title: Digital Technologies in Crop Production: A Scoping Review with Transferability Analysis for Central Asia
abstract: This scoping review maps 224 empirical studies (205 from a structured Scopus search, 2020–2026, plus 19 from a targeted Central Asia supplement) across four digital technology domains for crop production: IoT and sensor-based systems, UAVs and remote sensing, machine learning and AI, and nanostructured agrochemicals. The review follows the PRISMA-ScR framework and pursues three research questions concerning documented effects and validation limitations (RQ1); cross-cutting barriers in human capital, data governance, and infrastructure (RQ2); and the state of empirical evidence from Central Asia and Kazakhstan relative to international findings (RQ3). Across all four domains, the strongest reported effects occur where the data-to-decision-to-action loop is closed and sustained over multiple seasons, yet most published metrics rest on single-season, single-site, or controlled-environment validation that overstates likely field portability. IoT and selected UAV and ML workflows are closest to operational readiness where maintenance, calibration, and advisory support are sustained. Nanostructured materials remain the least mature domain in agronomic terms. For Central Asia, foundational monitoring and salinity-oriented remote sensing are the most immediately transferable elements; intervention-grade ML and integrated digital systems require local calibration, extension infrastructure, and multi-season field validation that are largely still absent. The review identifies the digital skills gap, incomplete data governance, and underreported total cost of ownership as the principal institutional barriers to scaling. Policy priorities include shifting from technical pilots to multi-season agronomic proof, building intermediary service capacity, and establishing transparent data-governance frameworks before large-scale procurement.

title: Predicting the potential distribution of Euryale ferox in China under future climate scenarios using MaxEnt modeling
abstract: Climate change poses a threat to both the natural habitat and the sustainable production of Euryale ferox , a valuable aquatic crop. To address this issue, our study employed an optimized Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) model to project the climatic suitability of E. ferox distribution in China for the 2030–2070 s under four climate scenarios. Utilizing 130 occurrence records of E. ferox and 20 ecological factors, we identified four primary factors influencing the distribution of E. ferox . The optimal conditions for E. ferox include elevations below 184.8 m, the temperature of the warmest season exceeds 25.7°C, the precipitation of the wettest month ranging between 167 and 718 mm, and precipitation over 9.5 mm in the driest month. The accuracy of the MaxEnt model predictions was comprehensively evaluated by the area under the ROC curve (AUC = 0.942) and the true skill statistic (TSS = 0.783), indicating its effectiveness in forecasting suitable environments. We also found that the current areas of highly and moderately suitable habitats are 0.909 × 10 5 km 2 and 3.324 × 10 5 km 2 , respectively. Compared to the current scenario, future projections indicate a significant increase in suitable areas. Furthermore, except for SSP245, the distribution centroid is projected to move southwestward then northward under other climate scenarios. These findings suggest that climate change may broadly benefit the expansion of E. ferox , offering critical insights for the formulation of regional conservation and cultivation strategies.

title: A Multi-Head UNet++ Framework with Fractional Differential Output Refinement for UAV Multispectral Crop Stress Mapping
abstract: This study presents a unified semantic segmentation framework for UAV-based multispectral crop stress mapping, focusing on the integration of water stress and rust disease conditions within a common label space. Unlike conventional approaches that address individual stress factors independently, the proposed framework harmonizes heterogeneous datasets with different annotation schemes into a single multi-class segmentation problem. To achieve this, UAV multispectral orthomosaics are processed using a patch-based strategy and a multi-head UNet++ architecture incorporating segmentation, edge-aware, and Signed Distance Transform (SDT) branches. In addition, a physics-informed output-space refinement module based on fractional partial differential equations (FPDE) is introduced to enhance spatial coherence and boundary preservation in the predicted maps. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework within the evaluated dataset setting, particularly in terms of boundary delineation, spatial consistency, and minority-class detection. The study highlights the feasibility of integrating heterogeneous stress conditions into a unified segmentation framework and provides a foundation for future research on scalable multi-source agricultural monitoring systems.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Integrated Environmental Resilience
venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly applied to environmental sustainability, yet research often treats agriculture, water management, and biodiversity conservation as separate domains. This chapter argues that AI can support integrated environmental resilience by enabling data-driven decision-making across these interconnected systems. It introduces a conceptual framework linking food production, water governance, and ecosystem protection through environmental informatics, machine learning, and geospatial analytics. The chapter reviews key applications in precision agriculture, hydrological forecasting, intelligent irrigation, and AI-based biodiversity monitoring, while examining how these tools support climate adaptation, resource efficiency, and ecosystem management. It also evaluates limitations including data bias, infrastructure gaps, and governance challenges. The chapter concludes that responsible, cross-sector AI can strengthen coordinated climate action and sustainable environmental management.

title: Optimised hybrid late fusion deep learning model for cashew disease classification
abstract: Introduction: Cashew farms are highly vulnerable to the attack of pests and plant diseases, which leads to massive losses in production and economic value. To diagnose the cashew disease, recent studies have explored deep learning methods; however, the existing models often have poor representative features and low generaliz-ability to different situations. Methods: As part of these solutions, we suggest a hybrid late-fusion architecture (combining EfficientNetV2-M and MobileNetV3-S) to extract the features and train them with XGBoost and CatBoost to give the classification, using the BOHB optimisation to make the hyper-parameter choices. By combin-ing MobileNetV3-S and EfficientNetV2-M, we can benefit from fine-grained visual information and computer efficiency. Result and discussion: The proposed model was experimented on the CCMT dataset comprising Anthracnose, Gummosis, Leaf Miner, Red Rust, and healthy leaf samples, achieving classification accuracies of 90% and 93%, with reduced computation times of 0.20 seconds for the XGBoost classifier and 0.07 seconds for the CatBoost classifier. As our findings show, boosting-based classifiers and efficient backbone networks can be combined to identify cashew disease effectively and computationally less complex.

title: Precision Application of Pesticides: Challenges, Opportunities, and Impacts on Crop Production Sustainability
abstract: Targeted precision application (PA) of pesticides has significant benefits for growers and to the environment by potentially reducing pesticide inputs by up to 90% without decreasing efficacy. Adoption of commercial sense-and-act PA systems is rapidly gaining in North America and other countries. However, incorporating the benefits of PA into risk assessment and risk mitigation of pesticides poses significant challenges. This paper summarizes collective perspectives from around fifty multidisciplined participants in a workshop to address these challenges and future opportunities of PA. It also addresses uncertainties and prospects such as pesticide resistance management, adoption by small growers, label language for targeted PA, and standards for testing PA equipment. The workshop participants identified necessary research, models, tools, and datasets for developing a framework to consider PA in pesticide regulation. Because of the complexity, collaboration among various stakeholders is needed to continue to realize benefits within the regulatory process. This collaboration is key to improved understanding of current commercially available precision spray systems used to apply herbicides in row crops as well as pesticides and foliar products in orchards, vineyards, and nursery crops. Moreover, it is essential to continue building collaborative momentum resulting in innovations in targeted PA technologies, thereby bringing the value of PA to all stakeholders to enhance the environmental sustainability and benefits for consumers and society.

title: Closing the Yield Gap: A Scalable Computer Vision Pipeline for In-Field Detection of Devastating Banana Diseases
abstract: Although bananas are planted due to food security of the world, they are subject to numerous fungi, bacteria and viruses that reduce the production. Visual method is the normative way through which banana plant infections are identified, and this technique lacks scalability, and it is arbitrary. A new method of deep learning that enables automatic, fast, and accurate identification and diagnosis of the pathogens that affect banana leaves is presented in this paper. Our hybrid Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model was developed and compared with EfficientNetB0 and ResNet50. The model has been trained using a diverse set of images and augmented even more using data augmentation methods. The model achieved great results of 98.7 percent precision and F1score of 0.986. It was capable of locating Black Sigatoka, Fusarium Wilt and Banana Xanthomonas Wilt. Gradientweighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) has validated that the model identifies biologically significant lesion areas, which enhance interpretability. The findings indicate that the framework is an effective and well-defined precision agriculture tool that simplifies easy response to quick action and possibly effective in identifying diseases in various crops.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Supervised and GRPO Fine-Tuning on Multimodal Visual Language Models for Plant Disease Identification
abstract: The use of AI in precision agriculture has the potential to improve food security significantly. According to recent research, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), specifically Vision Language Models (VLMs), can detect plant illnesses more accurately than the most advanced Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). However, accessibility is restricted by the use of large proprietary models. A wide range of VLMs, from open-weight models to effective proprietary models, are rigorously compared in this study and refined using Supervised FineTuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Our findings show a clear hierarchy of performance. The finetuned Gemini 2.5 Pro outperformed all prior benchmarks, achieving a new state-of-the-art performance on the Apple dataset (98.64%). Notably, Gemini 2.5 Flash maintained its superiority on the Corn dataset (93.66%), indicating that even within the same model family, performance varies across datasets. The quantized open-weights models, on the other hand, had severe difficulties. Gemma 3, fine-tuned with SFT and GRPO, failed to generalize and achieved accuracy below 30%, whereas Llama 3.2 led the open category with 68.61% on corn. Furthermore, while GRPO improved reasoning in Qwen 3.0 VL, it led to hallucination issues in smaller models such as Gemma. This paper delineates the trade-offs between model accessibility and diagnostic accuracy in agricultural contexts. In agricultural situations, this research outlines the trade-offs between diagnostic accuracy and model accessibility.

title: VLLFL: A Vision-Language Model Based Lightweight Federated Learning Framework for Smart Agriculture
Autonomous Weed Detection and Removal System using CNN and Python-Controlled Embedded Platform
abstract: Meeting the rising demand for sustainable agriculture and lowering work in the fields, intelligent external plant control systems are becoming increasingly necessary. This document describes autonomous external plant recognition and elimination systems using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) combined with a Python-driven embedded platform. The system being proposed makes use of a camera attached to a moving robot to take live pictures of the field. The images are then analyzed by a CNN model to distinguish between crops and weeds with accuracy. After identification, an embedded controller sends a signal to the mechanical actuator for weed removal. The model is qualified for running on the ESP32 platform which is a low-computation complexity platform and capable of real-time performance with an inference time of less than a second per image. Testing shows great classification accuracy, with even better precision and recall when field conditions vary. The system drastically cuts down on chemical herbicide use and manual labor, which is in line with farming practices that are environmentally friendly. The technique presented offers a cheap, extendable, and effective tool for precision farming. It can be used by small and medium-sized farms.

title: WS-DINO: A DINOv2-Based Weed Segmentation Method with Feature Priors and Spatial Fusion
abstract: Weed segmentation is a fundamental task in precision agriculture, essential for targeted intervention and sustainable farming. However, achieving accurate segmentation remains challenging due to the high visual similarity between weeds and crops, as well as the ambiguous, fine-grained boundaries often present in complex field environments. To address this, we present WS-DINO, a novel weed segmentation network built upon the DINOv2 vision foundation model. Our framework introduces two key innovations: (1) a Feature Prior Module that leverages a Canny-guided refinement process to extract and inject fine-grained cues related to weed texture, morphology, and boundaries into specific blocks of the Vision Transformer; and (2) a Spatial Feature Fusion Module that leverages convolutional layers to generate multi-scale spatial features, which are then fused with the semantically rich token features from DINOv2, effectively compensating for the Transformer’s limitations in capturing local spatial details. Comprehensive evaluation on the public PhenoBench dataset shows that WS-DINO achieves an mIoU of 88.67% and outperforms the evaluated benchmark methods. Moreover, on the challenging MotionBlurred dataset, WS-DINO reaches 88.75% mIoU, showing stable performance under motion blur and degraded visual conditions.

title: A Root Foundation Model for Zero-Shot Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Foundation models pre-trained on massive datasets have demonstrated impressive performance, but in some specialised domains have been found to have lower accuracy. Domain-specific foundation models target a particular domain such as retinal or plant images. These domain-specific models have shown inconsistent results and the benefit to root segmentation is unknown. We train and evaluate the first domainspecific foundation model for root segmentation. Evaluation uses a leave-one-dataset-out design across nine diverse root datasets with two architectures. Applied zero-shot to unseen datasets, the root foundation model achieves 92% of fine-tuned Dice on average (0.636 versus 0.698), with 5 of 9 datasets above 90%. With 10 patches of few-shot fine-tuning, the root foundation model recovers 95% of its full-data Dice on average, versus 69% for a general pre-trained model. At low patch counts the general pre-trained model often failed to converge, with 5 of 9 datasets giving Dice below 0.05 at 3 patches, while the root foundation model produced Dice above 0.47 on every dataset and patch count. With full target-data fine-tuning, the two perform comparably, with mean improvements of +0.011 Dice for MobileSAM and +0.022 for M2F Swin-S, neither significant (Wilcoxon p = 0.150 and 0.064). We release our pre-trained MobileSAM root foundation model for use with RootPainter, enabling fully automatic root segmentation on new datasets with an ordinary laptop or desktop computer, with no need for annotation or training.

title: Hard Attention Mechanism Integrated with VGG16 for High-Precision Tomato Leaf Disease Classification
Integrating deep learning and field validation into a decision support system for Northern Corn Leaf Blight management in maize
abstract: Northern Corn Leaf Blight (NCLB; also, Turcicum Leaf Blight, TLB), caused by Exserohilum turcicum (teleomorph: Setosphaeria turcica), is one of the most destructive foliar diseases of maize worldwide, often causing severe yield losses under favorable conditions. We developed a maize-specific, web-based Decision Support System (DSS) for real-time NCLB detection and management ( https://maize-nclb.streamlit.app/ ), integrating advanced deep-learning for automated diagnosis and fungicide advisory. Among thirteen Machine-learning and deep-learning models evaluated for classification, the Visual Geometry Group 16-layer convolutional neural network (VGG16) outperformed all others, achieving 94.0% accuracy, with balanced precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.94, and an AUC-ROC of 0.93. Confusion matrix analysis revealed minimal misclassification, with only 12 errors out of 357 samples, confirming the model's high reliability in distinguishing healthy and infected plants, while Grad-CAM visualizations consistently highlighted biologically meaningful lesion regions, supporting the model's interpretability and alignment with plant pathological symptoms. Field validation of DSS-guided fungicide recommendations (Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% w/w SC) demonstrated significant benefits, reducing disease incidence to 6.8% compared with 67.4% in controls, achieving 90% disease reduction, and enhancing grain yield by 35.4% (8.55 t/ha), with a favorable cost-benefit ratio of 1:2.49. Seasonal disease progression analysis further confirmed DSS effectiveness, with cumulative disease burden reduced by approximately 85% compared with untreated control. These results highlight the potential of integrating deep-learning with field-validated management strategies into a practical DSS, demonstrating its potential for precision disease management in maize.

title: A Lightweight Deep Learning Model for Plant Disease Detection Using Quantized YOLOv8n
abstract: Identifying crop diseases plays an important role in sustaining farming output, as it directly impacts food security. In recent years, neural network-based approaches have gained growing interest within the agricultural sector, specifically in detecting diseases, given that manual inspection is often impractical at a large scale. This highlights the need for edge-ready models capable of running on limited resource hardware, widely deployed in rural settings. This study investigates the application of post-training quantization to optimize YOLOv8n and evaluates the impact of int8 quantization on model performance using two datasets of varying complexity: PlantDoc and Tomato Disease. The results demonstrate that quantization achieves approximately a 50% reduction in model size and 15-25% improvement in inference speed, while maintaining 96-99% of the original detection accuracy.

title: An Uncertainty-Aware Attention-Based Residual U-Net for Cochineal Insect Segmentation
abstract: The quantification of uncertainty in image segmentation tasks has become essential to improve the reliability and applicability of computer vision systems. Two main approaches emerge: the standard training of the model and the integration of uncertainty directly into the loss function during training. This comparative study evaluates these two methodologies on the ResAtt-SE-UNet architecture for scale segmentation (Dactylopius opuntiae), a destructive pest of the prickly pear cactus. The experiment uses our original Tunisian database, comprising 451 annotated cactus images. The results show that the approach integrating uncertainty during training significantly improves accuracy by 4.19% (from 69.73% to 72.66%), while maintaining comparable performance in terms of Dice (66.78% against 66.77%). In the agricultural context, this approach offers better calibration of predictions and enhanced explainability, thanks to XAI analysis. The measured epistemic uncertainty (0.0099, 0.0505) indicates a high confidence of the model, while the random uncertainty (0.0490) mainly reveals ambiguities inherent to agricultural data. These results highlight the importance of integrating uncertainty quantification from the training phase for applications in precision agriculture, particularly in automated pest detection, where the reliability of predictions is paramount.

title: A study on plant recognition based on leaf image visualization systems
abstract: Accurate plant recognition is essential for biodiversity, ecological studies, and even the future of agriculture. Traditional methods are often slow and labor-intensive and rely heavily on experts. That’s why automated solutions have become so important. This survey looks at how artificial intelligence is changing the game for plant leaf recognition. It’s all about deep learning, machine learning, and image processing. Convolutional neural networks—think VGG16, ResNet50, DenseNet201 are some examples of models used in this field. Ensemble models and generative approaches add another layer, making systems more robust by expanding data diversity. Preprocessing steps like edge detection, morphological operations, background removal, and even generating synthetic data give the models a real boost in accuracy. For feature extraction, researchers lean on texture, shape, and color descriptors, while explainable AI tools like Grad-CAM make it easier to understand why models make certain decisions. This survey gathers the latest methods, tracks how they perform on different datasets, and points out both the challenges and the big opportunities ahead for building plant recognition systems that are efficient, accurate, and scalable. • Comprehensive review of machine learning and deep learning methods for plant recognition using leaf images. • Comparative analysis of preprocessing, feature extraction, and classification techniques used in recent studies. • Systematic overview of widely used public leaf image datasets and evaluation metrics. • Identification of key challenges, research gaps, and limitations in existing plant recognition systems. • Discussion of future research directions for accurate, interpretable, and deployable leaf-based identification models.

title: Real-World Tomato Leaf Disease Detection: A Comparative Study of YOLOv5–YOLOv12
abstract: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L.) production is threatened by foliar diseases that can cause severe yield and quality losses if not detected early. To support practical monitoring, this paper compares six YOLO small variants for real-world tomato disease detection using a manually annotated bounding-box dataset collected in open fields and greenhouses. Under a unified training/evaluation protocol, YOLOv5s, YOLOv8s, YOLOv9s, YOLOv10s, YOLOv11s, and YOLOv12s are benchmarked using mAP@0.5, mAP@0.5:0.95, precision, recall, and F1-score, alongside deployability indicators (speed, model size, FLOPs). The results highlight clear accuracy–efficiency trade-offs and provide guidance for selecting models for mobile/edge tomato disease monitoring.

title: Integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic investigation reveals that graphene oxide reduces nicosulfuron detriment in sweet corn
A Secure Federated Transfer Learning Approach for Cotton Leaf Disease Classification Using Deep Learning Neural Networks
abstract: Cotton, often referred to as ‘white gold,’ plays a vital role in agricultural economies, particularly in Bangladesh, where many livelihoods depend on farming. Despite favourable soil conditions, adequate water resources and a suitable climate, cotton production is frequently reduced by leaf diseases and pest infestations. As most cotton diseases primarily affect plant leaves, early and accurate detection is essential. Conventional visual inspection by farmers or agricultural experts is slow and prone to errors due to the similarity of disease symptoms. To address these challenges, this study proposes a federated transfer learning-based cotton leaf disease detection system that enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without sharing raw image data. Pre-trained deep learning architectures, including VGG-16, VGG-19, Inception-V3 and Xception, are fine-tuned locally on client devices, and their model updates are aggregated using a federated optimization strategy to build a robust global model. This approach preserves data privacy while leveraging the feature learning capability of transfer learning. The experimental results demonstrate that the federated Xception model achieved the highest accuracy of 98.70%, and was deployed in a smart web-based application for privacy-preserving and real-time disease prediction. The proposed system provides reliable cotton disease diagnosis and can be extended to other crops for secure and automated leaf disease detection in distributed agricultural environments.

title: Temporal Sensitivity of In-Season Crop Classification: An Explainable Multi-Year Sentinel-2 Analysis in Western Australia
abstract: Accurate in-season crop type mapping is critical for agricultural monitoring and yield assessment, yet most operational products remain proprietary, post-seasonal or insufficiently tested across contrasting seasons. This study presents an open and transferable framework that quantifies how in-season crop classification skills evolve through the growing season across the southwest agricultural region of Western Australia (WA) using a multi-temporal (2020–2024) Sentinel-2 derived vegetation indices (VIs) time-series. Six crop classes (i.e., wheat, barley, canola, lupins, pasture, and fallow) were evaluated using extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) and long short-term memory (LSTM) models under a leave-one-year-out cross-validation (LOYOCV) design. Classification performance increased progressively through the season, with a marked improvement in late winter (late August to early September). In LOYOCV, overall agreement with the reference dataset exceeded 90% once vegetation-index observations through August were included, indicating that reliable in-season mapping was achievable before harvest. Canola was separated consistently from mid-season onwards, whereas reliable discrimination between wheat and barley required later phenological information. Independent field-based testing was used to assess true crop identification accuracy for the three externally observed classes: wheat, barley, and canola. In this test set, precision was highest for canola (0.93), followed by wheat (0.82) and barley (0.71). These field-based results supported the main temporal pattern observed in the LOYOCV analysis, particularly the strong mid-season separability of canola and the persistent confusion between wheat and barley. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) showed thatVIs centred on late winter contributed most strongly to model predictions, consistent with peak phenological divergence among crop types. These results identify a phenologically meaningful decision window for in-season crop mapping and provide a multi-year benchmark for evaluating temporal transferability in Mediterranean broadacre systems.

title: ECO-TRACK: A Smart Agricultural Platform for Soil Health Analysis, Medicinal Plant Identification, and Market Guidance
Enhancing tomato disease identification via UPSGAN: an advanced cycleGAN-based image augmentation approach
Swin-HViT for accurate crop disease prediction using an adaptive hybrid transformer model
abstract: Agriculture plays a pivotal role in global economic growth, yet it faces significant challenges from pests and crop diseases. Early detection is crucial for preventing large-scale crop losses and ensuring food security. This study introduces an adaptive hybrid transformer model, Swin-HViT, which integrates the strengths of a vision transformer (ViT) and a Swin transformer to accurately predict crop diseases. While ViT captures global image features, the Swin Transformer excels at extracting fine-grained local details. To effectively integrate global and local feature, an adaptive fusion mechanism based on a trainable MLP is introduced, enabling dynamic feature weighting within the hybrid architecture. Evaluated on two benchmark datasets, Corn and PlantDoc, our model achieved accuracies of 99.03% and 83.07%, respectively, surpassing recent works. Here, we demonstrate the effectiveness of combining complementary transformer architectures to improve disease identification in diverse agricultural settings. The code, data and the hybrid model are available at https://github.com/hema2107/Swin-HViT .

title: Background Bias Assessment and Mitigation in Plant Disease Detection Using EfficientNet-B0 with Image Processing
abstract: Plant disease detection using deep learning has achieved remarkable accuracies exceeding 99% on benchmark datasets. However, these metrics may mask a critical vulnerability: models may be taking advantage of false background correlations instead of learning real pathological features. This study presents a systematic investigation of background bias in plant disease detection through a two-stage training framework with quantitative validation. We propose a three-condition evaluation protocol testing models on original, leaf-only, and background-only images to directly measure background dependency. Our approach combines standard transfer learning using EfficientNet-B0 and manipulation of background information during optimization. Experimental results on the PlantVillage dataset (20,638 images, 15 disease classes) show that while our model achieves 98.97% accuracy on the original images and maintains 96.62% accuracy on leaf-only images, the performance drops to $2 3. 5 8 \%$ on background-only images. The calculated background bias (BBC) coefficient of 0.762 indicates that a large part of the model’s predictive performance depends on leaf-related features rather than background distortions. This research offers clear evidence that even with the most advanced models, environmental shortcuts can be leveraged, and this highlights the importance of bias evaluation. The approach that has been used has laid a foundation for the development of agricultural AI that is ready for deployment. The implementation, models, and evaluation process are all publicly available.

title: Multi-Scale Feature Rectification for Crop Leaf Disease Segmentation in Complex Scenarios
abstract: Crop leaf disease segmentation in complex natural environments remains challenging because lesion regions often exhibit substantial scale variation, blurred boundaries, and severe background interference. To address these issues, this study proposes a Multi-Scale Feature Rectification Network (MFR-Net) for crop leaf disease segmentation. The proposed network adopts an EfficientNetV2-S-based encoder to extract hierarchical features, incorporates a hybrid attention mechanism to enhance lesion-sensitive spatial and channel representations, introduces a Cross-Window Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (CWASPP) module to strengthen multi-scale contextual modeling, and employs a Feature Rectification Module (FRM) in the decoder to alleviate semantic inconsistency during cross-level feature fusion. Experiments on a Kaggle-derived benchmark constructed from the unaugmented data folder of the public Leaf Disease Segmentation Dataset, containing 588 diseased-leaf images and 588 corresponding binary lesion masks, showed that MFR-Net achieved the highest mIoU of 74.27% and the highest Recall of 87.61% among the compared methods, and maintained competitive Dice performance (84.25%) with 25.10 M parameters and 37.55 G FLOPs. Ablation results further confirmed the effectiveness of the proposed design, with CWASPP providing the most notable individual contribution. Additional experiments were conducted on an independent Apple Leaf Dataset comprising 3197 image–mask pairs, collected under mixed controlled and natural field-like imaging conditions. The results showed competitive performance under a different data distribution, and robustness evaluation further verified stable performance under severe noise, blur, darkness, and contrast variation. All experiments were implemented in PyTorch 2.11.0 (CUDA 12.8) on a workstation equipped with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060 Ti GPU (8 GB). These results indicate that MFR-Net provides an effective and robust solution for crop leaf disease segmentation in complex agricultural scenarios.

title: Analysis of Lightweight CNN Models for Multi-Crop Leaf Disease Classification
abstract: Quick and precise plant disease detection is a key aspect in precision agriculture, particularly in resource-sensitive and field-scale settings. Whereas deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have proven to be very effective in leaf disease detection, most existing models rely on computationally intensive architectures that restrict real-time deployment. In this paper, a controlled comparative benchmark of two widely used lightweight CNNs (ResNet50 and InceptionV3) is presented for multi-crop leaf disease classification. An evidence-based preprocessing pipeline, including systematic data cleaning and Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE), is employed to optimize lesion visibility and feature consistency. Both models are trained on tomato and potato leaf disease classes from the PlantVillage dataset using transfer learning and evaluated under identical experimental conditions. The results indicate that ResNet50 converges stably with lower computational overhead, while InceptionV3 demonstrates stronger discrimination of complex disease patterns. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) is included as an experimental interpretability tool to qualitatively analyze model attention. Although the generated heatmaps are not always precise, they provide useful insights into disease-relevant regions influencing predictions. Overall, the findings highlight the trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability when deploying lightweight CNN architectures for practical multi-crop disease diagnosis.

title: Continual Learning across multiple domains via a Dynamic Expandable and Mergeable Model
AgroVeda: Deep Learning Based Crop Disease Prediction and Adaptive Recommendation System
abstract: Conventional methods adopted for the diagnosis of plant diseases rely heavily on the visual inspection and laboratory testing of the plant. This not only consumes a lot of time but also requires the skills of a specialist. Contributing to the delay in the diagnosis of the health of the crop, many smallscale farmers face hindrances in obtaining qualitative diagnosis. Despite the development of a few digital models being initiated in assisting with the diagnosis of diseases, they still face challenges related to the rigid rule-based system, inability to represent the diversity of diseases, inability to conduct real-time analysis, and inadequate guidance on corrective measures. To counter such limitations, this paper introduces a mobile prediction and recommendation system for plant disease management using deep learning algorithms. The proposed method uses a convolutional neural network (CNN) algorithm for plant disease prediction through leaf image analysis using a smartphone camera. Following prediction, the system provides accurate crop-related recommendations, such as treatment procedures, dosage, and prevention, to reduce disease occurrence. In this technology, predictive analysis combined with a sophisticated recommendation engine will help you make better informed early decisions and to have the ability to intervene if needed at your convenience. Experimental analysis shows that this proposed method helps in efficient disease prediction and relevant recommendations, leading to better crop management and a reduction in agricultural losses.

title: Hybrid Spatial-Temporal Attention Networks for Plant Disease Classification: a Benchmarking Study of Deep Learning Architectures
abstract: The accurate plant disease identification strategies can be critical for crop productivity and food security. This paper benchmarks several deep learning architectures for plant disease classification on the PlantVillage dataset with$\mathbf{6 1, 4 8 6}$images and 38 disease categories. The individual models assessed include typical CNNs (VGG19, ResNet50, DenseNet121, and EfficientNetB0/B4), a tailored CNN baseline, hybrids (CNN+Attention and CNN+LSTM), a CNN-LSTM-Temporal Attention architecture, and a transformer-like MAE-ViT. ResNet50 yields the highest accuracy of 99.39%. The best result in terms of accuracy (98.88%) was achieved by the proposed CNN+Attention model based on a spatial attention module applied after the CNN feature extractor and aimed at learning to attend to relevant regions in the image for disease. The training time for this model was also reported to be the lowest at 66.1 minutes. The CNN+LSTM model, which feed spatial feature maps to a bidirectional LSTM to capture multi-region dependencies, acquires 98.59% in 68.6 minutes. The CNN-LSTM-Temporal Attention variant adds this with a temporal attention layer that runs over the full sequence of LSTM outputs, achieving 98.15% in 82.9 minutes. MAE-ViT manages 89.37% only, showing that transformer designs need big and varying datasets to stay fit against structured agricultural images. Results demonstrate that hybrid CNN architectures deliver competitive accuracy with reduced computational overhead, with CNN+Attention offering the optimum accuracy-efficiency tradeoff for real-time and on-the-edge agricultural monitoring.

title: Semantic segmentation of Earth observation data

Transformative Energy-Efficient Edge-Optimised Multimodal Deep Learning Framework for Pest Management and Severity Analysis in Tea Plants
venue: ACM Transactions on Embedded Computing Systems
abstract: Recurrent infestations reduce yield and quality in Indian tea cultivation. Early visual symptoms under field conditions are often obscured by low light, high humidity, and leaf occlusion, limiting the reliability of conventional vision-based classifiers to controlled settings. Diverse field environments further degrade performance and constrain deployment on standard edge hardware. The multimodal, edge-optimised framework integrates RGB pest imagery with real-time environmental data for robust on-site monitoring . A hybrid CNN–Transformer backbone captures fine pest-specific textures and long-range contextual cues, while an attention-driven fusion layer adaptively incorporates temperature, humidity, and illumination signals. A key contribution is the custom dual-mode edge hardware , integrating dedicated CNN and Transformer accelerators with sensor co-processors. Hierarchical on-chip SRAM buffers reduce memory energy by \(200\times\) , supported by energy-aware scheduling. The system enables offline solar-powered inference in connectivity-limited settings and cloud-assisted synchronisation for periodic model updates. The dataset comprises 1,520 field-collected pest images , augmented to 7,600 samples across five classes . Environmental conditioning preserves 85.5% accuracy under combined perturbations, whereas unimodal inference degrades to 77.9% (approximately 15% error reduction). Hardware–algorithm co-design confines inference latency to 25 ms with 0.12 J energy per inference. Energy consumption remains 60% lower than Jetson Nano deployment. The formulation demonstrates that deployment-aware multimodal conditioning stabilises agricultural edge inference under energy, latency, and environmental constraints.

title: Multi-Modal Learning with Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Crop Analysis: A Comprehensive Review
venue: International Journal of Pattern Recognition and Artificial Intelligence
abstract: In modern agriculture, artificial intelligence (AI) is doing excellent work in crop monitoring, crop disease detection, crop yield prediction, and crop stress assessment. Various techniques such as deep learning, generative models, vision transformers, explainable AI (XAI), multimodal fusion, etc., have helped in building intelligent crop analysis. This paper provides the comparative crop analysis of various crop species, data modes, and environmental conditions for the review of benchmark studies for the current framework, experimental methodologies, and datasets. The important challenges and open issues identified are limited field datasets, class imbalance, dataset bias, high computational complexity, privacy concerns, etc. Based on these, we suggested future work that can include foundation models, digital twin techniques, federated learning, multimodal frameworks, and interpretability architecture. This review provides a review for creating reliable, scalable, and sustainable AI-driven crop analysis systems. In addition to that, the survey seeks to give researchers and AI practitioners a comprehensive analysis of the current situation.

abstract: • Parallel branches resolve conflicts: masked autoencoder & edge-aware contrastive path. • Random coordinate attention fuses cross-branch features via gradient-modulated keys. • Gradient histogram alignment balances objectives, boosting classification and detection. • Validated on ImageNet, COCO, VOC, Birdsnap, Leaf Disease datasets shows SOTA performance.

title: Optimizing EfficientNet-Lite with Quantization-Aware Training for Lightweight Plant Disease Detection
abstract: Crop losses from plant diseases are widespread across farmed land, causing financial harm alongside threats to food security. It is critically important to grow crops well so that sicknesses are found early, with high reliability. Recent advances in machine learning, especially those image-based deep learning models, are now spotting sick leaves with high classification accuracy. Still, top-level CNNs tend to incur high computational cost while being unsuitable for resource-constrained devices commonly used in farming. This work looks at a learner setup for spotting crop illnesses by using EfficientNet-Lite with Quantization-Aware Training. Instead of trading precision for speed, it tries matching both well under real-world limits. Training is performed using a mix of pepper, potato, and tomato leaf pictures from various plant illness collections. Results tested under controlled settings revealed that the FP32 version handles categorization well. After QAT tuning at INT8 precision, the size dropped, yet forward times stayed relatively low, QAT finetuning further improved classification accuracy to 99.54 % at INT8 precision. A close look at the error layout exposed clear divisions across sickness types, hinting at how well the method remains robust under real conditions. Findings show QATenhanced EfficientNet-Lite works well in farm and phone settings. It runs on typical mobile units plus rural edge devices. Performance fits common use cases across both areas for spotting crop illnesses. Its role in smart farming demonstrates practical viability when deployed on agricultural edge devices.

title: Evaluating the Performance of Pre-Trained Neural Networks in Identifying Plant Diseases
abstract: Apple trees are susceptible to numerous diseases. A timely and precise diagnosis is required to safeguard crop quality. One of the newest innovations in deep learning (DL), convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are known to be very effective for a wide variety of applications, including the diagnosis of plant diseases. The models were developed using a PlantVillage dataset containing three distinct classes of apple diseases and a healthy class. Low-level characteristics are inadequate for discrimination and domain-specific classification. Existence of a semantic gap between features of low-level, as machine understanding and features of high-level, as human perception. The primary objective of this study is to conduct a comparative analysis of contemporary network models, including AlexNet, GoogleNet, Inception V3, MobileNet-v2, ShuffleNet, and SqueezeNet, with the aim of fine-tuning them. The final three layers of deep neural networks are processed using a pre-trained deep convolutional neural network technique and a fine-tuned methodology. The models' performance was assessed using a variety of factors, such as batch size, number of epochs, initial learning rate, and optimization technique. In a multiclass statistical evaluation of the models, precision, recall, and F-score were utilized. Using AlexNet, GoogleNet, Inception V3, MobileNet-v2, ShuffleNet, and SqueezeNet, the implemented models attained disease classification accuracy rates of$\mathbf{9 7. 0 5 \%}, \mathbf{9 9. 7 9 \%}, \mathbf{9 8. 3 2 \%}, \mathbf{9 9. 1 6 \%}$, 99.37%, and 98.95%, respectively. These rates were greater than those of conventional handmade feature-based approaches. The GoogleNet model performed better than other deep-learning models, with an F -score of 99.82%, a precision of 99.74%, an accuracy of 99.79%, and a recall of 99.9%. The deep CNN model may be able to identify Apple plant illnesses in real-time agricultural systems, based on the accuracy scores in the detection of Apple leaf diseases. Thus, the deep CNN model is encouraging and might have a big influence on accurately diagnosing illnesses.

title: Plant Diseases Prediction using CNN
abstract: Plant diseases continue to be a critical constraint to global agricultural productivity, diminishing crop yield, degrading quality, and directly impacting farmer livelihoods. Early and accurate detection of plant diseases is essential for minimizing economic losses and enabling timely intervention. This paper proposes an intelligent plant disease prediction framework driven by a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) optimized for leafimage classification. The model achieves a classification accuracy of 93%, demonstrating strong discriminative capability across diseased and healthy samples. To extend its practical relevance, the system is integrated with a multilingual conversational agent that provides region-specific guidance, including disease explanations, preventive measures, and recommended pesticides or fertilizers. The chatbot delivers context-aware responses in local languages, thereby improving accessibility for rural users and reducing dependence on agricultural experts. The overall architecture includes a structured preprocessing pipeline, deep feature extraction, confidence-driven prediction, and an interactive assistance layer tailored for low-resource deployment.
